17.3.5 Building the Calendar Heatmaps

grouped <- attacks %>%
  count(wkday, hour) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  na.omit()

ggplot(grouped,
       aes(hour,
           wkday,
           fill = n)) +
geom_tile(color = "white",
          size = 0.1) +
theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") +
coord_equal() +
scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                    low = "sky blue",
                    high = "dark blue") +
labs(x = NULL,
     y = NULL,
     title = "Attacks by weekday and time of day") +
theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
      plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
      legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 6) )














TipThings to learn from the code chunk




a tibble data table called grouped is derived by aggregating the attack by wkday and hour fields.
a new field called n is derived by using group_by() and count() functions.
na.omit() is used to exclude missing value.
geom_tile() is used to plot tiles (grids) at each x and y position. color and size arguments are used to specify the border color and line size of the tiles.
theme_tufte() of ggthemes package is used to remove unnecessary chart junk. To learn which visual components of default ggplot2 have been excluded, you are encouraged to comment out this line to examine the default plot.
coord_equal() is used to ensure the plot will have an aspect ratio of 1:1.
scale_fill_gradient() function is used to creates a two colour gradient (low-high).



Then we can simply group the count by hour and wkday and plot it, since we know that we have values for every combination there’s no need to further preprocess the data.


17.3.6 Building Multiple Calendar Heatmaps
Challenge: Building multiple heatmaps for the top four countries with the highest number of attacks. 


17.3.7 Plotting Multiple Calendar Heatmaps
Step 1: Deriving attack by country object
In order to identify the top 4 countries with the highest number of attacks, you are required to do the followings:

count the number of attacks by country,
calculate the percent of attackes by country, and
save the results in a tibble data frame.


attacks_by_country <- count(
  attacks, source_country) %>%
  mutate(percent = percent(n/sum(n))) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))

Step 2: Preparing the tidy data frame
In this step, you are required to extract the attack records of the top 4 countries from attacks data frame and save the data in a new tibble data frame (i.e. top4_attacks).

top4 <- attacks_by_country$source_country[1:4]
top4_attacks <- attacks %>%
  filter(source_country %in% top4) %>%
  count(source_country, wkday, hour) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(source_country = factor(
    source_country, levels = top4)) %>%
  na.omit()



17.3.8 Plotting Multiple Calendar Heatmaps
Step 3: Plotting the Multiple Calender Heatmap by using ggplot2 package.

ggplot(top4_attacks,
       aes(hour,
           wkday,
           fill = n)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white",
          size = 0.1) +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                    low = "sky blue",
                    high = "dark blue") +
  facet_wrap(~source_country, ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
     title = "Attacks on top 4 countries by weekday and time of day") +
  theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 6) )

text:
17.4 Plotting Cycle Plot
In this section, you will learn how to plot a cycle plot showing the time-series patterns and trend of visitor arrivals from Vietnam programmatically by using ggplot2 functions. 

17.4.1 Step 1: Data Import
For the purpose of this hands-on exercise, arrivals_by_air.xlsx will be used.
The code chunk below imports arrivals_by_air.xlsx by using read_excel() of readxl package and save it as a tibble data frame called air.

air <- read_excel("../Data/arrivals_by_air.xlsx")



17.4.2 Step 2: Deriving month and year fields
Next, two new fields called month and year are derived from Month-Year field.

air$month <- factor(month(air$`Month-Year`),
                    levels=1:12,
                    labels=month.abb,
                    ordered=TRUE)
air$year <- year(ymd(air$`Month-Year`))



17.4.3 Step 3: Extracting the target country
Next, the code chunk below is use to extract data for the target country (i.e. Vietnam)

Vietnam <- air %>%
  select(`Vietnam`,
         month,
         year) %>%
  filter(year >= 2010)



17.4.4 Step 4: Computing year average arrivals by month
The code chunk below uses group_by() and summarise() of dplyr to compute year average arrivals by month.

hline.data <- Vietnam %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(avgvalue = mean(`Vietnam`))



17.4.5 Step 5: Plotting the cycle plot
The code chunk below is used to plot the cycle plot.

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data=Vietnam,
            aes(x=year,
                y=`Vietnam`,
                group=month),
            colour="black") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept=avgvalue),
             data=hline.data,
             linetype=6,
             colour="red",
             size=0.5) +
  facet_grid(~month) +
  labs(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
       title = "Visitor arrivals from Vietnam by air, Jan 2010-Dec 2019") +
  xlab("") +
  ylab("No. of Visitors") +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica")

rice <- read_csv("../Data/rice.csv")

rice %>%

title: 21 Choropleth Mapping with R
text:
Choropleth mapping involves the symbolisation of enumeration units — such as countries, provinces, states, counties, or census units — using area patterns or graduated colours. For example, a social scientist may use a choropleth map to portray the spatial distribution of the aged population of Singapore by Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary.
In this chapter, you will learn how to plot functional and truthful choropleth maps using an R package called tmap.






Tip

text:
21.2 Getting Started
In this hands-on exercise, the key R package used is tmap. Besides tmap, four other R packages will be used:

readr for importing delimited text files,
tidyr for tidying data,
dplyr for wrangling data, and
sf for handling geospatial data.

Among the four, readr, tidyr, and dplyr are part of the tidyverse package.
The code chunk below will install and load these packages in RStudio.

pacman::p_load(sf, tmap, tidyverse)







Note



Notice that we only need to install tidyverse rather than readr, tidyr, and dplyr individually.

title: 21 Choropleth Mapping with R
text:
21.3 Importing Data into R

21.3.1 The Data
Two datasets will be used to create the choropleth map:

Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (Web) (i.e. MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL) in ESRI shapefile format. It can be downloaded from data.gov.sg. This is a geospatial dataset consisting of the geographical boundary of Singapore at the planning subzone level. The data is based on the URA Master Plan 2014.
Singapore Residents by Planning Area / Subzone, Age Group, Sex and Type of Dwelling, June 2011-2020 in CSV format (i.e. respopagesextod2011to2020.csv). This is an aspatial data file, downloadable from the Department of Statistics, Singapore. Although it does not contain any coordinate values, its PA and SZ fields can be used as unique identifiers to geocode to the MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL shapefile.



21.3.2 Importing Geospatial Data into R
The code chunk below uses the st_read() function of the sf package to import the MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL shapefile into R as a simple feature data frame called mpsz.

mpsz <- st_read(dsn = "../Data/geospatial",
                layer = "MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL")

21.3.3 Importing Attribute Data into R
Next, we will import the respopagesextod2011to2020.csv file into RStudio and save it as an R data frame called popdata.
This task will be performed using the read_csv() function of the readr package, as shown below.

popdata <- read_csv("../Data/respopagesextod2011to2020.csv")



21.3.4 Data Preparation
Before a thematic map can be prepared, you are required to build a data table containing year-2020 values. The data table should include the variables PA, SZ, YOUNG, ECONOMY ACTIVE, AGED, TOTAL, and DEPENDENCY:

YOUNG: age group 0-4 up to age group 20-24,
ECONOMY ACTIVE: age group 25-29 up to age group 60-64,
AGED: age group 65 and above,
TOTAL: all age groups, and
DEPENDENCY: the ratio of the young and aged populations against the economically active group.


21.3.4.1 Data Wrangling
The following data-wrangling and transformation functions will be used:

pivot_wider() of the tidyr package, and
mutate(), filter(), group_by(), and select() of the dplyr package.


popdata2020 <- popdata %>%
  filter(Time == 2020) %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(`POP` = sum(`Pop`)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = AG,
              values_from = POP) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[3:6])
         + rowSums(.[12])) %>%
  mutate(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(.[7:11]) +
           rowSums(.[13:15])) %>%
  mutate(`AGED` = rowSums(.[16:21])) %>%
  mutate(`TOTAL` = rowSums(.[3:21])) %>%
  mutate(`DEPENDENCY` = (`YOUNG` + `AGED`)
         / `ECONOMY ACTIVE`) %>%
  select(`PA`, `SZ`, `YOUNG`,
         `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, `AGED`,
         `TOTAL`, `DEPENDENCY`)



21.3.4.2 Joining the Attribute Data and Geospatial Data
Before we can perform the geo-relational join, one extra step is required: convert the values in the PA and SZ fields to uppercase. This is because the values of PA and SZ contain a mix of upper- and lowercase letters, whereas SUBZONE_N and PLN_AREA_N are in uppercase.

popdata2020 <- popdata2020 %>%
  mutate(across(c(PA, SZ), toupper)) %>%
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)

Next, left_join() of dplyr is used to join the geographical data and attribute table using the planning subzone name (i.e. SUBZONE_N and SZ) as the common identifier.

mpsz_pop2020 <- left_join(mpsz, popdata2020,
                          by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ"))







NoteThings to learn from the code chunk above:




left_join() of dplyr is used with the mpsz simple feature data frame as the left table to ensure that the output is also a simple feature data frame.




write_rds(mpsz_pop2020, "../Data/mpszpop2020.rds")

title: 21 Choropleth Mapping with R
section: 21.4 Choropleth Mapping Geospatial Data Using tmap
text:
21.4 Choropleth Mapping Geospatial Data Using tmap
Two approaches can be used to prepare a thematic map with tmap:

Plotting a thematic map quickly using qtm().
Plotting a highly customisable thematic map using tmap elements.


21.4.1 Plotting a Choropleth Map Quickly Using qtm()
The easiest and quickest way to draw a choropleth map with tmap is by using qtm(). It is concise and provides good default visualisation in many cases.
The code chunk below draws a cartographically standard choropleth map.

tmap_mode("plot")
qtm(mpsz_pop2020,
    fill = "DEPENDENCY")














NoteThings to learn from the code chunk above:




tmap_mode() with the "plot" option produces a static map. For interactive mode, use the "view" option.
The fill argument is used to map the attribute (i.e. DEPENDENCY).





21.4.2 Creating a Choropleth Map Using tmap’s Elements
Despite its usefulness for drawing a choropleth map quickly and easily, the disadvantage of qtm() is that it makes the aesthetics of individual layers harder to control. To draw a high-quality cartographic choropleth map, tmap’s drawing elements should be used.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by Planning Subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA)\n and Population data from Department of Statistics (DOS)",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))








In the following sub-sections, we will share with you the tmap functions used to plot these elements.

21.4.2.1 Drawing a Base Map
The basic building block of tmap is tm_shape() followed by one or more layer elements such as tm_fill() and tm_polygons().
In the code chunk below, tm_shape() defines the input data (i.e. mpsz_pop2020) and tm_polygons() draws the planning subzone polygons.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons()










21.4.2.2 Drawing a Choropleth Map Using tm_polygons()
To draw a choropleth map showing the geographical distribution of a selected variable by planning subzone, we simply assign the target variable (e.g. Dependency) to tm_polygons().

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY")














NoteThings to learn from tm_polygons():




The default interval binning used to draw the choropleth map is called "pretty". A detailed discussion of the data-classification methods supported by tmap is given in the next sub-section.
The default colour scheme is YlOrRd from ColorBrewer. You will learn more about colour schemes shortly.
By default, missing values are shaded in grey.





21.4.2.3 Drawing a Choropleth Map Using tm_fill() and tm_borders()
In fact, tm_polygons() is a wrapper around tm_fill() and tm_borders(). tm_fill() shades the polygons using the default colour scheme, and tm_borders() adds the borders of the shapefile onto the choropleth map.
The code chunk below draws a choropleth map using tm_fill() alone.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY")








Notice that the planning subzones are shaded according to their respective dependency values.
To add the boundaries of the planning subzones, tm_borders() is used, as shown below.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders(lwd = 0.01,
             fill_alpha = 0.1)








Notice that light-grey border lines have been added to the choropleth map.
The alpha argument defines transparency as a number between 0 (fully transparent) and 1 (fully opaque). By default, the alpha value of col is used (normally 1).
Besides alpha, there are three other arguments for tm_borders():

col — border colour,
lwd — border line width (default is 1), and
lty — border line type (default is "solid").




21.4.3 Data Classification Methods of tmap
Most choropleth maps employ some method of data classification. The point of classification is to take a large number of observations and group them into data ranges or classes.
tmap provides ten data-classification methods: fixed, sd, equal, pretty (default), quantile, kmeans, hclust, bclust, fisher, and jenks.
To specify a data-classification method, the style argument of tm_fill() or tm_polygons() is used.

21.4.3.1 Plotting Choropleth Maps with Built-in Classification Methods
The code chunk below shows a Jenks data classification using 5 classes.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "jenks",
        n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








The next code chunk uses the equal classification method.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "equal",
        n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








Notice that the distribution produced by the quantile method is more evenly distributed than the one produced by the equal method.






Warning



Maps Lie!
DIY: Using what you have learned, prepare choropleth maps using different classification methods supported by tmap and compare the differences.
DIY: Prepare choropleth maps using the same classification method but with different numbers of classes (e.g. 2, 6, 10, 20). Compare the resulting maps — what can you observe?




DIY 1: Comparing Different Classification Methods
The code chunk below produces four choropleth maps of the DEPENDENCY variable using four different classification styles, all with n = 5 classes.

equal_map <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Equal Interval")

quantile_map <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Quantile")

jenks_map <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "jenks",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Jenks (Natural Breaks)")

sd_map <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "sd",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Standard Deviation")

tmap_arrange(equal_map, quantile_map, jenks_map, sd_map,
             asp = 1, ncol = 2)








Observations:

Equal Interval divides the data range into bins of equal width. Because the DEPENDENCY variable contains a few extreme outliers (max ≈ 19), most subzones end up squeezed into the lowest class, leaving the map looking flat and uninformative.
Quantile places an equal number of subzones in each class. This produces a visually balanced map with strong colour contrast, but it can exaggerate small differences between similar values.
Jenks (Natural Breaks) finds break points that minimise within-class variance and maximise between-class variance. The resulting map highlights genuine clusters in the data and is often the best general-purpose choice.
Standard Deviation centres the classes around the mean. It is useful for revealing how unusual each subzone is relative to the average, but it relies on the data being roughly normally distributed.

The key lesson: the same data can produce very different-looking maps depending on the classification method. A cartographer’s choice can mislead the reader — hence “Maps Lie”.


DIY 2: Varying the Number of Classes
The code chunk below produces four quantile choropleth maps with n = 2, 6, 10, and 20 classes.

n2_map <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 2,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("n = 2 classes")

n6_map <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 6,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("n = 6 classes")

n10_map <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("n = 10 classes")

n20_map <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 20,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("n = 20 classes")

tmap_arrange(n2_map, n6_map, n10_map, n20_map,
             asp = 1, ncol = 2)








Observations:

n = 2 produces a binary map — every subzone is either “above” or “below” the median. Spatial patterns are easy to see at a glance, but most of the detail is lost.
n = 6 strikes a reasonable balance between readability and detail. Broad regional patterns remain visible while finer variation is still distinguishable.
n = 10 begins to reveal more local variation, but the human eye struggles to differentiate so many similar shades of blue, especially on small polygons.
n = 20 is essentially unreadable as a thematic map. The colour ramp is too granular for visual comparison, and adjacent classes become indistinguishable.

Rule of thumb: most cartographers recommend between 4 and 7 classes for a sequential colour scheme. Fewer classes oversimplify the data; more classes overwhelm the reader.


21.4.3.2 Plotting a Choropleth Map with Custom Breaks
For all the built-in styles, the category breaks are computed internally. To override these defaults, the breakpoints can be set explicitly via the breaks argument of tm_fill(). Note that in tmap, the breaks include both a minimum and a maximum. As a result, to end up with n categories, n + 1 elements must be specified in the breaks vector (the values must be in increasing order).
Before we begin, it is good practice to compute descriptive statistics for the variable before setting breakpoints. The code chunk below computes and displays the descriptive statistics of the DEPENDENCY field.

summary(mpsz_pop2020$DEPENDENCY)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
 0.1111  0.7147  0.7867  0.8585  0.8763 19.0000      92 


Based on the results, we set breakpoints at 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, and 0.90. In addition, we include a minimum and maximum, which we set at 0 and 1.00. Our breaks vector is therefore c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00).
Now we plot the choropleth map using the code chunk below.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)











21.4.4 Colour Scheme
tmap supports colour ramps that are either user-defined or chosen from a set of predefined colour ramps from the RColorBrewer package.

21.4.4.1 Using ColorBrewer Palettes
To change the colour, assign the preferred colour to the values argument of tm_scale_intervals(), as shown below.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "quantile",
        n = 5,
        values = "brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








Notice that the choropleth map is now shaded in green.
To reverse the colour shading, add a "-" prefix.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "quantile",
        n = 5,
        values = "-brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)











21.4.5 Map Layouts
Map layout refers to the combination of all map elements into a cohesive map. Map elements include, among others, the objects to be mapped, the title, the scale bar, the compass, margins, and aspect ratios. Colour settings and data-classification methods (covered earlier) relate to the palette and breakpoints, which affect how the map looks.

21.4.5.1 Map Legend
In tmap, several tm_legend() options are provided to change the placement, format, and appearance of the legend.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "jenks",
        n = 5,
        values = "brewer.greens"),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by Planning Subzone \n(Jenks classification)")










21.4.5.2 Map Style
tmap allows a wide variety of layout settings to be changed via tmap_style().
The code chunk below uses the classic style.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          style = "quantile",
          palette = "-Greens") +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("classic")










21.4.5.3 Cartographic Furniture
Besides map style, tmap also provides arguments for drawing other map furniture such as compass, scale bar, and grid lines.
In the code chunk below, tm_compass(), tm_scale_bar(), and tm_grid() are used to add a compass, scale bar, and grid lines to the choropleth map.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by Planning Subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA)\n and Population data from Department of Statistics (DOS)",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))








To reset the default style, refer to the code chunk below.

tmap_style("white")




21.4.6 Drawing Small Multiple Choropleth Maps
Small multiple maps, also referred to as facet maps, are composed of many maps arranged side-by-side and sometimes stacked vertically. Small multiple maps enable the visualisation of how spatial relationships change with respect to another variable, such as time.
In tmap, small multiple maps can be plotted in three ways:

by assigning multiple values to at least one of the aesthetic arguments,
by defining a group-by variable in tm_facets(), and
by creating multiple stand-alone maps with tmap_arrange().


21.4.6.1 By Assigning Multiple Values to at Least One Aesthetic Argument
In this example, small multiple choropleth maps are created by defining ncols in tm_fill().

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill(c("YOUNG", "AGED"),
          style = "equal",
          palette = "Blues") +
  tm_layout(legend.position = c("right", "bottom")) +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("white")








In this example, small multiple choropleth maps are created by assigning multiple values to at least one aesthetic argument.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(c("DEPENDENCY", "AGED"),
              style = c("equal", "quantile"),
              palette = list("Blues", "Greens")) +
  tm_layout(legend.position = c("right", "bottom"))










21.4.6.2 By Defining a Group-by Variable in tm_facets()
In this example, multiple small choropleth maps are created using tm_facets().

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          style = "quantile",
          palette = "Blues",
          thres.poly = 0) +
  tm_facets(by = "REGION_N",
            free.coords = TRUE) +
  tm_layout(legend.show = FALSE,
            title.position = c("center", "center"),
            title.size = 20) +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5)










21.4.6.3 By Creating Multiple Stand-alone Maps with tmap_arrange()
In this example, multiple small choropleth maps are created by combining stand-alone maps with tmap_arrange().

youngmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("YOUNG",
              style = "quantile",
              palette = "Blues")

agedmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("AGED",
              style = "quantile",
              palette = "Blues")

tmap_arrange(youngmap, agedmap, asp = 1, ncol = 2)











21.4.7 Mapping Spatial Objects Meeting a Selection Criterion
Instead of creating small multiple choropleth maps, you can also use a selection function to map spatial objects meeting a particular selection criterion.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020[mpsz_pop2020$REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION", ]) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          style = "quantile",
          palette = "Blues",
          legend.hist = TRUE,
          legend.is.portrait = TRUE,
          legend.hist.z = 0.1) +
  tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE,
            legend.height = 0.45,
            legend.width = 5.0,
            legend.position = c("right", "bottom"),
            frame = FALSE) +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5)

title: 22 Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text:
Proportional symbol maps (also called graduated symbol maps) belong to a family of thematic maps that use the visual variable of size to represent magnitude differences for a discrete, abruptly changing phenomenon — for example, counts of people or events. As with choropleth maps, they can be drawn in two flavours: a classed version (range-graded or graduated symbols) and an unclassed version (true proportional symbols, where the symbol area is directly proportional to the underlying attribute value).
In this hands-on exercise, we will build a proportional symbol map that visualises the number of wins recorded at Singapore Pools’ outlets using the R package tmap.

sgpools <- read_csv("../Data/SGPools_svy21.csv")

22.4.3 Creating an sf data frame from an aspatial data frame
The chunk below converts the sgpools tibble into a simple feature data frame using st_as_sf() from the sf package.

sgpools_sf <- st_as_sf(sgpools,
                       coords = c("XCOORD", "YCOORD"),
                       crs = 3414)







NoteThings to learn from the arguments above:




The coords argument expects the x-coordinate column first, followed by the y-coordinate column.
The crs argument requires the coordinate reference system in EPSG format. EPSG: 3414 is the Singapore SVY21 Projected Coordinate System. EPSG codes for other countries can be found at epsg.io.

title: 22 Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text:
22.5 Drawing a Proportional Symbol Map
To produce an interactive proportional symbol map in R, we switch tmap into its view mode.
The chunk below turns the interactive mode on.

tmap_mode("view")


22.5.1 It all started with an interactive point symbol map
The chunk below produces a simple interactive point symbol map — every outlet appears as a red bubble of the same size.

tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "red",
             size = 1,
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)







22.5.2 Let’s make it proportional
To turn the map into a proportional symbol map, we map a numeric variable to the size aesthetic. In the chunk below, the variable Gp1Gp2 Winnings is assigned to size.

tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "red",
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)








22.5.3 Let’s give it a different colour
The map can be enhanced further by using the fill aesthetic to encode a categorical variable. In the chunk below, OUTLET TYPE is mapped to the bubble fill colour, so outlets and branches are visually distinguishable.

tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "OUTLET TYPE",
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)









22.5.4 Faceted maps with synchronised navigation
A neat — and somewhat lesser-known — feature of tmap’s view mode is that it also supports faceted plots. The sync argument inside tm_facets() produces multiple side-by-side maps whose zoom and pan are linked.

tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "OUTLET TYPE",
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1) +
  tm_facets(by = "OUTLET TYPE",
            nrow = 1,
            sync = TRUE)
















Before ending the session, it is good practice to switch tmap’s viewer back to plot mode.

tmap_mode("plot")

title: 23 Analytical Mapping
text:
23.2 Getting Started

23.2.1 Installing and loading packages
Using the steps learned in the previous lesson, install and load the sf, tmap, and tidyverse packages into the R environment.

pacman::p_load(tmap, tidyverse, sf)



23.2.2 Importing data
For the purpose of this hands-on exercise, a prepared dataset called NGA_wp.rds will be used. The dataset is a polygon feature data frame providing information on water points in Nigeria at the LGA level. You can find the dataset in the rds sub-directory of the hands-on data folder.
Using the appropriate function, import NGA_wp.rds into the R environment.

NGA_wp <- read_rds("../Data/NGA_wp.rds")

title: 23 Analytical Mapping
text:
23.3 Basic Choropleth Mapping

23.3.1 Visualising distribution of non-functional water points
Plot a choropleth map showing the distribution of non-functional water points by LGA.

p1 <- tm_shape(NGA_wp) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "wp_functional",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = c("right", "bottom"))) +
  tm_borders(lwd = 0.1,
             fill_alpha = 1) +
  tm_title("Distribution of functional water points by LGAs")


p2 <- tm_shape(NGA_wp) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "total_wp",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = c("right", "bottom"))) +
  tm_borders(lwd = 0.1,
             fill_alpha = 1) +
  tm_title("Distribution of total water points by LGAs")


tmap_arrange(p2, p1, nrow = 1)

title: 23 Analytical Mapping
text:
23.4 Choropleth Map for Rates
In our readings we have seen the importance of mapping rates rather than counts. The reason is simple: water points are not equally distributed in space. If we do not account for how many water points are located in an area, we end up mapping the total water point size rather than our topic of interest.

23.4.1 Deriving proportion of functional and non-functional water points
We will tabulate the proportion of functional water points and the proportion of non-functional water points in each LGA. In the following code chunk, mutate() from the dplyr package is used to derive two fields, namely pct_functional and pct_nonfunctional.

NGA_wp <- NGA_wp %>%
  mutate(pct_functional = wp_functional / total_wp) %>%
  mutate(pct_nonfunctional = wp_nonfunctional / total_wp)



23.4.2 Plotting a map of rate
Plot a choropleth map showing the distribution of the percentage of functional water points by LGA.

tm_shape(NGA_wp) +
  tm_polygons("pct_functional",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = c("right", "bottom"))) +
  tm_borders(lwd = 0.1,
             fill_alpha = 1) +
  tm_title("Rate map of functional water points by LGAs")

title: 23 Analytical Mapping
text:
23.5 Extreme Value Maps
Extreme value maps are variations of common choropleth maps where the classification is designed to highlight extreme values at the lower and upper ends of the scale, with the goal of identifying outliers. These maps were developed in the spirit of spatialising EDA — that is, adding spatial features to commonly used approaches in non-spatial EDA (Anselin 1994).

23.5.1 Percentile Map
The percentile map is a special type of quantile map with six specific categories: 0–1%, 1–10%, 10–50%, 50–90%, 90–99%, and 99–100%. The corresponding break points can be derived using the base R quantile() command, passing an explicit vector of cumulative probabilities as c(0, .01, .1, .5, .9, .99, 1). Note that the begin and end points need to be included.

23.5.1.1 Data Preparation
Step 1: Exclude records with NA using the code chunk below.

NGA_wp <- NGA_wp %>%
  drop_na()

Step 2: Create a customised classification and extract values.

percent <- c(0, .01, .1, .5, .9, .99, 1)
var <- NGA_wp["pct_functional"] %>%
  st_set_geometry(NULL)
quantile(var[, 1], percent)

       0%        1%       10%       50%       90%       99%      100% 
0.0000000 0.0000000 0.2169811 0.4791667 0.8611111 1.0000000 1.0000000 








Important



When variables are extracted from an sf data frame, the geometry is extracted as well. For mapping and spatial manipulation, this is the expected behaviour, but many base R functions cannot deal with the geometry. Specifically, quantile() will return an error. As a result, st_set_geometry(NULL) is used to drop the geometry field.




23.5.1.2 Why write functions?
Writing a function has three big advantages over copy-and-paste:

You can give a function an evocative name that makes your code easier to understand.
As requirements change, you only need to update the code in one place, rather than in many.
You eliminate the chance of making incidental mistakes when copying and pasting (for example, updating a variable name in one place but not in another).

Source: Chapter 19: Functions of R for Data Science.


23.5.1.3 Creating the get.var function
First, we will write an R function to extract a variable (e.g. wp_nonfunctional) as a vector out of an sf data frame.

Arguments:

vname: variable name (as character, in quotes)
df: name of the sf data frame

Returns:

v: vector of values (without a column name)



get.var <- function(vname, df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>%
    st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[, 1])
  return(v)
}



23.5.1.4 A percentile mapping function
Next, we will write a percentile mapping function using the code chunk below.

percentmap <- function(vnam, df, legtitle = NA, mtitle = "Percentile Map") {
  percent <- c(0, .01, .1, .5, .9, .99, 1)
  var <- get.var(vnam, df)
  bperc <- quantile(var, percent)
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons() +
    tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons(vnam,
                title = legtitle,
                breaks = bperc,
                palette = "Blues",
                labels = c("< 1%", "1% - 10%", "10% - 50%",
                           "50% - 90%", "90% - 99%", "> 99%")) +
    tm_borders() +
    tm_layout(main.title = mtitle,
              title.position = c("right", "bottom"))
}



23.5.1.5 Test driving the percentile mapping function
To run the function, type the code chunk shown below.

percentmap("total_wp", NGA_wp)








Note that this is just a bare-bones implementation. Additional arguments — such as the title and legend positioning, to name a few — could be passed to customise various features of the map.



23.5.2 Box Map
In essence, a box map is an augmented quartile map with an additional lower and upper category. When there are lower outliers, the starting point for the breaks is the minimum value, and the second break is the lower fence. In contrast, when there are no lower outliers, the starting point for the breaks will be the lower fence, and the second break is the minimum value (there will be no observations falling in the interval between the lower fence and the minimum value).

ggplot(data = NGA_wp,
       aes(x = "",
           y = wp_nonfunctional)) +
  geom_boxplot()









Display summary statistics on a choropleth map using the basic principles of a boxplot.
To create a box map, a custom breaks specification will be used. However, there is a complication: the break points for the box map vary depending on whether lower or upper outliers are present.


23.5.2.1 Creating the boxbreaks function
The code chunk below defines an R function that creates break points for a box map.

Arguments:

v: vector with observations
mult: multiplier for IQR (default 1.5)

Returns:

bb: vector with 7 break points, computed using quartiles and fences



boxbreaks <- function(v, mult = 1.5) {
  qv <- unname(quantile(v))
  iqr <- qv[4] - qv[2]
  upfence <- qv[4] + mult * iqr
  lofence <- qv[2] - mult * iqr
  # initialise break points vector
  bb <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = 7)
  # logic for lower and upper fences
  if (lofence < qv[1]) {  # no lower outliers
    bb[1] <- lofence
    bb[2] <- floor(qv[1])
  } else {
    bb[2] <- lofence
    bb[1] <- qv[1]
  }
  if (upfence > qv[5]) {  # no upper outliers
    bb[7] <- upfence
    bb[6] <- ceiling(qv[5])
  } else {
    bb[6] <- upfence
    bb[7] <- qv[5]
  }
  bb[3:5] <- qv[2:4]
  return(bb)
}



23.5.2.2 Creating the get.var function
The code chunk below defines an R function to extract a variable as a vector out of an sf data frame.

Arguments:

vname: variable name (as character, in quotes)
df: name of the sf data frame

Returns:

v: vector of values (without a column name)



get.var <- function(vname, df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>% st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[, 1])
  return(v)
}



23.5.2.3 Test driving the newly created function
Let’s test the newly created function.

var <- get.var("wp_nonfunctional", NGA_wp)
boxbreaks(var)

[1] -56.5   0.0  14.0  34.0  61.0 131.5 278.0




23.5.2.4 Box map function
The code chunk below defines an R function to create a box map.

Arguments:

vnam: variable name (as character, in quotes)
df: simple features polygon layer
legtitle: legend title
mtitle: map title
mult: multiplier for IQR

Returns:

a tmap element (plots a map)



boxmap <- function(vnam, df,
                   legtitle = NA,
                   mtitle = "Box Map",
                   mult = 1.5) {
  var <- get.var(vnam, df)
  bb <- boxbreaks(var)
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons() +
    tm_shape(df) +
    tm_fill(vnam, title = legtitle,
            breaks = bb,
            palette = "Blues",
            labels = c("lower outlier",
                       "< 25%",
                       "25% - 50%",
                       "50% - 75%",
                       "> 75%",
                       "upper outlier")) +
    tm_borders() +
    tm_layout(main.title = mtitle,
              title.position = c("left", "top"))
}


tmap_mode("plot")
boxmap("wp_nonfunctional", NGA_wp)

text:
31.2 Getting Started
For the purpose of this hands-on exercise, the following R packages will be used.

tidyverse provides a collection of functions for performing data science task such as importing, tidying, wrangling data and visualising data. It is not a single package but a collection of modern R packages including but not limited to readr, tidyr, dplyr, ggplot, tibble, stringr, forcats and purrr.
lubridate provides functions to work with dates and times more efficiently.
ggthemes is an extension of ggplot2. It provides additional themes beyond the basic themes of ggplot2.
gtExtras provides some additional helper functions to assist in creating beautiful tables with gt, an R package specially designed for anyone to make wonderful-looking tables using the R programming language.
reactable provides functions to create interactive data tables for R, based on the React Table library and made with reactR.
reactablefmtr provides various features to streamline and enhance the styling of interactive reactable tables with easy-to-use and highly-customizable functions and themes.



Show the code
if (!requireNamespace("remotes", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("remotes")
if (!requireNamespace("dataui", quietly = TRUE)) {
  remotes::install_github("timelyportfolio/dataui")
}
if (!requireNamespace("reactablefmtr", quietly = TRUE)) {
  remotes::install_github("kcuilla/reactablefmtr")
}

reactablefmtr, gt, gtExtras, tidyverse)

text:
31.3 Importing Microsoft Access Database

31.3.1 The Data Set
For the purpose of this study, a personal database in Microsoft Access mdb format called Coffee Chain will be used.


31.3.2 Importing Database into R
In the code chunk below, odbcConnectAccess() of the RODBC package is used to import a database query table into R.






Note



Before running the code chunk, you need to change the R system to the 32-bit version. This is because odbcConnectAccess() is based on 32-bit and not 64-bit.




Show the code
library(RODBC)
con <- odbcConnectAccess2007('../Data/Coffee Chain.mdb')
coffeechain <- sqlFetch(con, 'CoffeeChain Query')
write_rds(coffeechain, "../Data/CoffeeChain.rds")
odbcClose(con)




31.3.3 Data Preparation
The code chunk below is used to import CoffeeChain.rds into R.


Show the code
coffeechain <- read_rds("../Data/CoffeeChain.rds")








Note



This step is optional if coffeechain is already available in R.


The code chunk below is used to aggregate Sales and Budgeted Sales at the Product level.


Show the code
product <- coffeechain %>%
  group_by(`Product`) %>%
  summarise(`target` = sum(`Budget Sales`),
            `current` = sum(`Sales`)) %>%
  ungroup()




31.3.4 Bullet Chart in ggplot2
The code chunk below is used to plot the bullet charts using ggplot2 functions.


Show the code
ggplot(product, aes(Product, current)) +
  geom_col(aes(Product, max(target) * 1.01),
           fill="grey85", width=0.85) +
  geom_col(aes(Product, target * 0.75),
           fill="grey60", width=0.85) +
  geom_col(aes(Product, target * 0.5),
           fill="grey50", width=0.85) +
  geom_col(aes(Product, current),
           width=0.35,
           fill = "black") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(y = target,
                    x = Product,
                    ymin = target,
                    ymax= target),
                width = .4,
                colour = "red",
                size = 1) +
  coord_flip()

title: 31 Information Dashboard Design: R Methods
text:
31.4 Plotting Sparklines Using ggplot2
In this section, you will learn how to plot sparklines by using ggplot2.

31.4.1 Preparing the Data


Show the code
sales_report <- coffeechain %>%
  filter(Date >= "2013-01-01") %>%
  mutate(Month = month(Date)) %>%
  group_by(Month, Product) %>%
  summarise(Sales = sum(Sales)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(Month, Product, Sales)


The code chunk below is used to compute the minimum, maximum and end of the month sales.


Show the code
mins <- group_by(sales_report, Product) %>%
  slice(which.min(Sales))
maxs <- group_by(sales_report, Product) %>%
  slice(which.max(Sales))
ends <- group_by(sales_report, Product) %>%
  filter(Month == max(Month))


The code chunk below is used to compute the 25 and 75 quantiles.


Show the code
quarts <- sales_report %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarise(quart1 = quantile(Sales,
                              0.25),
            quart2 = quantile(Sales,
                              0.75)) %>%
  right_join(sales_report)




31.4.2 Sparklines in ggplot2
The code chunk used.


Show the code
ggplot(sales_report, aes(x=Month, y=Sales)) +
  facet_grid(Product ~ ., scales = "free_y") +
  geom_ribbon(data = quarts, aes(ymin = quart1, max = quart2),
              fill = 'grey90') +
  geom_line(size=0.3) +
  geom_point(data = mins, col = 'red') +
  geom_point(data = maxs, col = 'blue') +
  geom_text(data = mins, aes(label = Sales), vjust = -1) +
  geom_text(data = maxs, aes(label = Sales), vjust = 2.5) +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = Sales), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.5) +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = Product), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 1.0) +
  expand_limits(x = max(sales_report$Month) +
                  (0.25 * (max(sales_report$Month) - min(sales_report$Month)))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 12, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0.1, 0)) +
  theme_tufte(base_size = 3, base_family = "Helvetica") +
  theme(axis.title=element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(), strip.text = element_blank())

31.5 Static Information Dashboard Design: gt and gtExtras Methods
In this section, you will learn how to create static information dashboard by using gt and gtExtras packages. Before getting started, it is highly recommended for you to visit the webpage of these two packages and review all the materials provided on the webpages at least once. You do not have to understand and remember everything provided but at least have an overview of the purposes and functions provided by them.

31.5.1 Plotting a Simple Bullet Chart
In this section, you will learn how to prepare a bullet chart report by using functions of gt and gtExtras packages.


Show the code
product %>%
  gt::gt() %>%
  gt_plt_bullet(column = current,
              target = target,
              width = 60,
              palette = c("lightblue",

text:
31.6 Sparklines: gtExtras Method
Before we can prepare the sales report by product by using gtExtras functions, the code chunk below will be used to prepare the data.


Show the code
report <- coffeechain %>%
  mutate(Year = year(Date)) %>%
  filter(Year == "2013") %>%
  mutate (Month = month(Date,
                        label = TRUE,
                        abbr = TRUE)) %>%
  group_by(Product, Month) %>%
  summarise(Sales = sum(Sales)) %>%
  ungroup()


It is important to note that one of the requirements of gtExtras functions is that almost exclusively they require you to pass data.frame with list columns. In view of this, the code chunk below will be used to convert the report data.frame into list columns.


Show the code
report %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarize('Monthly Sales' = list(Sales),
            .groups = "drop")

title: 31 Information Dashboard Design: R Methods
section: 31.7 Interactive Information Dashboard Design: reactable and reactablefmtr Methods
text:
31.7 Interactive Information Dashboard Design: reactable and reactablefmtr Methods
In this section, you will learn how to create interactive information dashboard by using reactable and reactablefmtr packages. Before getting started, it is highly recommended for you to visit the webpage of these two packages and review all the materials provided on the webpages at least once. You done not have to understand and remember everything provided but at least have an overview of the purposes and functions provided by them.
In order to build an interactive sparklines, we need to install dataui R package by using the code chunk below.


Show the code
if (!requireNamespace("dataui", quietly = TRUE)) {
  remotes::install_github("timelyportfolio/dataui")
}


Next, you will need to load the package onto R environment by using the code chunk below.


Show the code
library(dataui)



31.7.1 Plotting Interactive Sparklines
Similar to gtExtras, to plot an interactive sparklines by using reactablefmtr package we need to prepare the list field by using the code chunk below.


Show the code
report <- report %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarize(`Monthly Sales` = list(Sales))


Next, react_sparkline will be to plot the sparklines as shown below.


Show the code
reactable(
  report,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkline(report)
    )
  )
)








31.7.2 Changing the Pagesize
By default the pagesize is 10. In the code chunk below, argument defaultPageSize is used to change the default setting.


Show the code
reactable(
  report,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkline(report)
    )
  )
)








31.7.3 Adding Points and Labels
In the code chunk below highlight_points argument is used to show the minimum and maximum values points and label argument is used to label first and last values.


Show the code
reactable(
  report,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkline(
        report,
        highlight_points = highlight_points(
          min = "red", max = "blue"),
        labels = c("first", "last")
        )
    )
  )
)








31.7.4 Adding Reference Line
In the code chunk below  statline  argument is used to show the mean line.


Show the code
reactable(
  report,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkline(
        report,
        highlight_points = highlight_points(
          min = "red", max = "blue"),
        statline = "mean"
        )
    )
  )
)








31.7.5 Adding Bandline
Instead adding reference line,  bandline  can be added by using the bandline argument.


Show the code
reactable(
  report,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkline(
        report,
        highlight_points = highlight_points(
          min = "red", max = "blue"),
        line_width = 1,
        bandline = "innerquartiles",
        bandline_color = "green"
        )
    )
  )
)








31.7.6 Changing from Sparkline to Sparkbar
Instead of displaying the values as sparklines, we can display them as sparkbars as shown below.


Show the code
reactable(
  report,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkbar(
        report,
        highlight_bars = highlight_bars(
          min = "red", max = "blue"),
        bandline = "innerquartiles",
        statline = "mean")
    )
  )
)
